This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Our goal is to make SciPy’s multivariate distributions interoperable with NumPy’s broadcasting conventions. We’ve observed that `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))` generates output of shape `(10, 4, 2, 3)`, where the last dimension comes from the gufunc signature `(n)`, and `size` only expands the leading axes. But we’re unsure if this behavior is formally specified or if other distributions like `multivariate_hypergeometric` (signature `(n),() -> (n)`) are expected to follow the same pattern. Are we safe to assume this is the intended semantics, or is this an undocumented convention?

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As part of the effort to upgrade SciPy's multivariate distribution capabilities, we are seeking assurance that any modifications will not diverge from the semantics established by NumPy's multivariate distribution functions. The specific unknown concerns the relationship between the `size` argument and the broadcasting of parameter arrays—such as the `pvals` matrix for multinomial or the covariance matrix for multivariate normal—especially when those parameters are not scalars. Clarification on how to formulate the gufunc signatures and expected output shapes for these scenarios would be highly valuable.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Just to give some context: SciPy is trying to extend its multivariate distributions while staying compatible with NumPy's current and future behavior. The tricky part is figuring out how the `size` argument should behave when the distribution parameters themselves get broadcast (e.g., some are vectors, some are matrices). We have a concrete example for `multinomial` that shows `size=(10,4,2)` produces an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`, where the last dimension comes from the gufunc signature. I'm wondering how we should generalize this pattern to `dirichlet`, `multivariate_normal`, and `multivariate_hypergeometric`.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.

 MPS 36.00 s

 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

I verified no CPU fallbacks via Activity Monitor, and even tried forcing `torch.mps.empty_cache()` — no improvement. Is this a known regression in recent PyTorch versions? Or does MPS not yet support efficient kernel fusion for the BERT architecture's multi-head attention pattern?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s

 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.

 import torch

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2

 x2 = x1[:, delay:]

 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

original_statement:
Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re evaluating how `size` interacts with broadcasting in multivariate distributions. In NumPy, `size` determines the batch dimensions but not the variate dimension—which is inferred from the distribution’s signature. However, we’re not sure whether this is a deliberate, documented design principle or merely an emergent consequence of current implementations. Without clarity, we risk introducing inconsistency across SciPy’s new distributions. Is this behavior part of the public API contract?

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: COMMIT_ADAPTIVE behavior varies with the device's low‑memory watermark and the timing of Python garbage collection, which can affect observed memory patterns.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

Additionally, I’d like to report that the same issue also occurs when using nn.RNN instead of nn.LSTM. Specifically, like:

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.
rephrased_statement: I’ve confirmed that disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled fixes the export issue on GPU — this strongly suggests the root cause lies in cuDNN’s fused kernels, particularly how they interact with fake tensor tracing. The cuDNN version is 90100, and the same problem occurs with nn.RNN, not just nn.LSTM — is this expected behavior for all cuDNN-backed RNN layers during export?

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I am trying to determine whether the `size` argument is intended to describe only the number of variates per broadcasted parameter configuration, or if it should also incorporate the dimensionality associated with the gufunc signature. Might the other multivariate distribution functions be adapted in the same way as the proposed multinomial broadcasting, treating the variate dimension separately from `size`?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As we extend broadcasting support in SciPy’s multivariate distributions, we need to clarify whether the `size` parameter should behave uniformly across all distributions—specifically, whether it should only govern the number of samples per parameter combination and exclude the intrinsic variate dimension (e.g., the `(n,)` in `(n),(n,n) -> (n)`). In NumPy’s current `multinomial`, `size=(10, 4, 2)` yields an output shape of `(10, 4, 2, 3)`, not `(10, 4, 2)`—so we’re uncertain if this pattern is canonical or accidental, and whether other distributions like `multivariate_normal` should follow suit.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I'm seeing BERT inference on MPS take roughly twice as long as on CPU—even though the GPU is clearly active (98% utilization, 15W+ power draw). The same code runs in under a second on CUDA, so I’m wondering if MPS just isn’t optimized for transformer attention patterns yet, or if there’s a hidden bottleneck I’m missing.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: In NumPy, `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=s)` produces an output with shape `s + (n,)`, where `s` is the broadcast shape of inputs and `(n,)` comes from the gufunc signature. But for `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=s)`, the output is `s + (mean.shape[-1],)`. I’m unsure whether this consistency is guaranteed or coincidental—should SciPy enforce this pattern, or is it an implementation detail we shouldn’t rely on?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

Additionally, I’d like to report that the same issue also occurs when using nn.RNN instead of nn.LSTM. Specifically, like:

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: When using `size` with NumPy’s multivariate distributions, does it only control the outer batch dimensions, leaving event dimensions (like the last axis in multinomial outputs) untouched? If so, how do we reconcile this with `multivariate_hypergeometric` or `dirichlet`—whose gufunc signatures suggest different broadcasting rules? We need clarity before implementing similar logic in SciPy.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Empirical run on a local environment required approximately 5–6 seconds of idle time for the adaptive commit path to allow object finalization and memory release.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: So, we're trying to upgrade SciPy's multivariate distribution suite while keeping everything in sync with NumPy's own multivariate APIs now and down the road. The knot we need to untie is how the `size` parameter interacts with broadcasting when the distribution's parameters aren't just scalars but arrays of various shapes (some 1‑D, some 2‑D). To make sense of it, I'm looking at the gufunc signatures that describe each distribution – like `multivariate_normal` being `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` – even though they aren't implemented as real gufuncs yet. The example from @bashtage's PR shows that broadcasting works for `multinomial`, but we still need to map that approach onto distributions like `dirichlet`, `multivariate_hypergeometric`, etc., so the output shapes make sense and `size` only controls the number of draws, not the variate dimensions.

I accidentally discovered that nn.Linear with datatype float16/bfloat16 can produce significant numerical errors on sliced tensors:
 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]
 assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 

 I got the output like this:
 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As we expand multivariate distribution support in SciPy, we’re evaluating whether `size` should consistently exclude the output event dimension across all distributions. For `multinomial`, we have: `size=(10,4,2)` + event dim `(3)` → `(10,4,2,3)`. But does `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(10,4,2))` behave the same? We don’t have certainty—there’s no public specification, and the gufunc signatures are internal. We’re trying to avoid making an irreversible API decision based on an assumption that might not hold across NumPy’s future releases.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: The current behavior of `size` in NumPy’s multivariate distributions seems to follow a pattern: output shape = `size` concatenated with the output dimension of the gufunc signature. But this is never explicitly stated. Since SciPy is expanding this API, we need to confirm: is this behavior intentional across all distributions? If we implement `size` differently for, say, `multivariate_hypergeometric`, will that break user expectations? We don’t know whether this is a standard or an implementation artifact.

I accidentally discovered that nn.Linear with datatype float16/bfloat16 can produce significant numerical errors on sliced tensors:
 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]
 assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 

 I got the output like this:
 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 If the type is bfloat16, the error is even greater:
 tensor(0.0078, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.bfloat16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 However, if the tensor is cloned after sliced x2 = x1[:, delay:].clone() or the type is float32, it will produce an error of exactly zero.
 tensor(0., device='cuda:0', grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 

 I don't know if this is an allowable margin of error or a bug.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: After seeing how rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2)) yields (10,4,2,3), I'm not sure whether other multivariate distributions should behave the same way. The gufunc signatures suggest a pattern, but I don't know if NumPy has made this an explicit API guarantee — or if we're just lucky it works this way.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Hey folks, as part of the ongoing SciPy effort to polish up our multivariate distributions and roll out a few new ones, we need to double‑check that any changes we make stay in step with NumPy's current and upcoming multivariate distribution API. The sticking point right now is the `size` argument: it seems to get tangled up with broadcasting when the distribution parameters are arrays (think 1‑D or 2‑D) instead of simple scalars. To get a handle on this, I'm looking at the gufunc‑style signatures for each distribution – e.g., `multivariate_normal` is `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` – even though they're not actual gufuncs yet. The PR by @bashtage adds broadcasting support to `multinomial`, letting you do something like `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))` and get an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`. The challenge now is to extend that broadcasting behavior to the other multivariate distribution functions so that `size` cleanly specifies the number of samples without accidentally adding extra dimensions from the parameter shapes.

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

I suspect the issue lies in how MPS translates Hugging Face’s token embedding + encoder stack into Metal shaders, possibly due to suboptimal kernel fusion or lack of support for sparse attention patterns. Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: A modified script that allows the adaptive commit to complete shows memory being freed after approximately 5‑6 seconds on a local setup.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re evaluating how to extend broadcasting rules to multivariate distributions like `multivariate_normal` and `dirichlet`, inspired by the new `multinomial` behavior. The key ambiguity is whether `size` controls only the batch dimension (excluding the event dimension) across all distributions. Since `multinomial`’s signature is `(),(n) -> (n)`, and `multivariate_normal` is `(n),(n,n) -> (n)`, should `size=(10,5)` in both cases produce outputs of shape `(10,5,n)`? Or do we need to treat covariance matrices differently? We don’t know if NumPy has a stated policy here.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: When designing new multivariate distributions in SciPy, we're uncertain whether `size` should be interpreted as controlling only the batch shape (excluding the variate dimension), as appears to be the case in NumPy’s `multinomial`. For instance, with `mean=(2,)` and `cov=(2,2)`, should `rng.multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(5, 3))` return shape `(5, 3, 2)`? We lack clarity on whether this is a formal API contract or an undocumented behavior we should avoid relying on.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Is NumPy’s `size` parameter in multivariate distributions strictly a batch shape specifier that *never* includes the event dimension (e.g., final axis like 3 in multinomial)? This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I'm working on the SciPy side of things to flesh out our multivariate distributions and want to be sure any improvements we add still line up with how NumPy currently does (and will do) its multivariate distributions. The tricky part is the `size` argument: it seems to interfere with broadcasting when the distribution parameters are arrays – sometimes they're 1‑D vectors, other times 2‑D matrices, not just single numbers. I'm using the gufunc‑style signatures as a guide (e.g., `multivariate_hypergeometric` is `(n),() -> (n)`) even though the code isn’t a real gufunc yet. The recent PR from @bashtage shows how to broadcast `multinomial` inputs, but we need to generalize that pattern for the rest of the distribution family so that `size` only determines the number of samples and doesn’t get mixed up with the shape of the parameter arrays.
