Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I'm seeing a 2x performance regression when running BERT inference on MPS compared to CPU, even though the MPS backend is active (98% GPU utilization, 15W power spike). The same code on CUDA achieves ~44x faster speeds. Is this expected given the current state of MPS optimization for transformer models, or is there a known bottleneck with embedding layers or attention kernel dispatch on Apple Silicon?

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement:
We will ensure that any improvements to SciPy’s multivariate distributions remain in lockstep with NumPy’s behavior by formalizing the interaction between the `size` parameter and broadcasting of distribution parameters. The relevant gufunc signatures—`dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`—serve as the blueprint. For example, using
```python
n = np.array([2,5,10,20]).reshape(-1,1)
pvals = np.array([[0.1,0.2,0.7],[0.8,0.2,0.0]])
rng = np.random.default_rng()
result = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))
```
produces an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`, where the first dimension is the number of variates per parameter combination, the next two dimensions are the broadcasted input shape, and the final dimension is the size of each variate. This broadcasting strategy will be consistently applied to all other multivariate distribution functions.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Hey folks, we're updating SciPy's multivariate distributions and want to make sure any new features still line up with how NumPy does its multivariate stuff. I'm a bit stuck on how the `size` argument should interact with broadcasting when some of the distribution parameters are 1‑D or 2‑D arrays instead of scalars.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're trying to unify broadcasting behavior across SciPy's multivariate distributions, but I'm uncertain: should size=(...) behave identically in multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(10,)) as it does in multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,))? The gufunc signatures suggest consistency is possible, but I don't know if NumPy intends for size to exclude the last dimension universally.

rephrased_statement: In an ad‑hoc validation of half‑precision arithmetic on CUDA I discovered that `nn.Linear` can emit divergent results when its input is a non‑contiguous view of a `float16` (or `bfloat16`) tensor.  The reproducible example seeds the random generator, creates `x1 = torch.randn(2,16,4, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)`, then extracts `x2 = x1[:, 2:]`.  A preliminary `torch.allclose` confirms the slices are numerically identical.  After casting a linear module to the same dtype (`net = nn.Linear(4,4).to("cuda").to(dtype=torch.float16)`), the forward passes yield `out1 = net(x1)` and `out2 = net(x2)`.  The diagnostic `print((out1[:, 2:] - out2).abs().max())` prints `tensor(0.0010, ...)`, and the following `assert torch.allclose` raises an error.  The phenomenon is exacerbated in `bfloat16` (`0.0078`).  A simple `clone()` on the slice or upgrading to `float32` restores exact equality.  I'm left wondering whether this behavior falls under the permissible error margin for half‑precision GEMM on strided tensors, or whether it reveals a latent bug in the ATen kernel implementations.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're trying to align SciPy's multivariate distribution enhancements with NumPy's broadcasting semantics, but I'm uncertain if the role of `size` in `rng.multinomial(..., size=...)` should be interpreted identically across distributions. For example, in `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(10, 4))`, does `size` still exclude the last dimension (the dimension of the mean vector), or should it fully determine the output shape? I don't know if this is a design choice we've inherited or one we need to explicitly define.

 import torch

original_statement:
Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Benchmark on a MacBook M1: CPU 18.38 s vs. MPS 36.00 s for batch size 64 using `BertForSequenceClassification` (see code snippet below).

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: A pull request by @bashtage introduces broadcasting support for the `multinomial` distribution, with example code illustrating variate generation using broadcasted inputs.

 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2

 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: To keep SciPy’s multivariate distribution suite compatible with NumPy’s semantics, we will adopt a broadcasting strategy that respects the `size` parameter and the gufunc‑style signatures of each distribution. The signatures—`dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`—guide how parameter arrays of different dimensions are combined. In practice, using `rng.multinomial` with `n = np.array([2,5,10,20]).reshape(-1,1)`, `pvals = np.array([[0.1,0.2,0.7],[0.8,0.2,0.0]])`, and `size=(10,4,2)` yields a shape `(10,4,2,3)`. This demonstrates that `size` controls the number of draws per broadcasted parameter set, while the trailing dimension reflects the outcome size. We will replicate this approach for `multivariate_normal`, `dirichlet`, and other distributions.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:

 import timeit

  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Given the recent broadcasting improvements to `multinomial`, we’re trying to understand whether the `size` parameter in NumPy’s multivariate distributions should be interpreted as controlling only the sample batch dimensions, with the variate dimension always appended independently. For example, in `(n),(n,n) -> (n)`, the result’s final dimension is fixed by the signature, not `size`. We don’t know if this is the universally expected behavior, and whether we’re safe to assume that `multivariate_normal` should follow the same pattern when we introduce broadcasting support—especially since no formal documentation explicitly defines this semantics.

In a minimal reproducible script I seed the RNG, allocate a `float16` tensor `x1` of shape `(2,16,4)` on CUDA, then create a delayed slice `x2 = x1[:, 2:]`.  A sanity check `torch.allclose(x1[:, 2:], x2)` passes, yet after moving a linear projection to the same dtype (`net = nn.Linear(4,4).to("cuda").to(dtype=torch.float16)`) the outputs diverge: `out1 = net(x1)`, `out2 = net(x2)`, and `print((out1[:, 2:] - out2).abs().max())` yields `tensor(0.0010, ...)` and the subsequent `assert torch.allclose(out1[:, 2:], out2)` triggers an `AssertionError`.  Switching the dtype to `bfloat16` inflates the discrepancy to `0.0078`.  Curiously, if I force a materialized copy (`x2 = x1[:, 2:].clone()`) or fall back to `float32`, the max difference collapses to zero.  Could this be an acceptable tolerance envelope for half‑precision linear layers on non‑contiguous inputs, or does it expose a latent bug in PyTorch's low‑precision GEMM handling for strided tensors?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Could it be that `size` specifies the count of draws for each broadcasted set of parameters, while the shape implied by the gufunc signature remains independent? If so, how should we reconcile this interpretation across dirichlet, multinomial, multivariate_normal, and multivariate_hypergeometric implementations?

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I don't know whether the `size` parameter is supposed to incorporate the gufunc output dimension when broadcasting multivariate distribution parameters (e.g., Dirichlet's alpha or Multivariate_normal's mean/cov), and I'm looking for clarification on how to generalize the approach used in the multinomial PR to the other distributions.

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

Additionally, I’d like to report that the same issue also occurs when using nn.RNN instead of nn.LSTM. Specifically, like:

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.
rephrased_statement: Disabling cuDNN fixes the export; likely cuDNN‑fused kernels aren't properly guarded during tracing with fake tensors, affecting LSTM and RNN alike.

 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2

 x2 = x1[:, delay:]

 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I'm uncertain whether the broadcasting rules demonstrated in @bashtage's multinomial pull request—where `size=(10,4,2)` yields an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`—apply unchanged to other SciPy multivariate distribution APIs. Specifically, how should we handle the interplay between `size` and the gufunc signatures listed (e.g., `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` for `multivariate_normal`) when the parameters are supplied as 1‑D or 2‑D arrays?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Is it normal for MPS to underperform CPU on BERT sequence classification? My benchmark shows 36s on MPS vs 18s on CPU, yet GPU usage is maxed out. The CUDA version is blazing fast at 0.82s, so it’s not the model. I suspect MPS isn’t properly offloading certain ops—maybe attention or embedding layers? Is there a known issue with transformer op dispatch on Apple Silicon?

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

Additionally, I’d like to report that the same issue also occurs when using nn.RNN instead of nn.LSTM. Specifically, like:

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.
rephrased_statement: Export fails with cuDNN-enabled RNN/LSTM layers using fake tensors, but works when cuDNN is disabled. cuDNN v90100 is in use. Could this be due to missing opaque kernel annotations during FX tracing for fused recurrent ops?

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Quick question: when we add broadcasting support to the other multivariate distribution methods, should the `size` kwarg reflect only the number of draws we want, or also the broadcasted shape of the input parameters (like the `(4,2)` part in the multinomial example)? I'm not clear on the expected semantics.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're trying to standardize the interface for multivariate distribution sampling in SciPy, particularly how `size` integrates with parameter broadcasting. Based on `multinomial`'s behavior in the PR, `size` controls the outer batch dimensions while leaving the output's last dimension (e.g., `n` in `(n)`) untouched. But we don’t know if this design was intentional for all distributions, or if `multivariate_normal` with `(n),(n,n)->(n)` should treat `size` differently when `mean` or `cov` are higher-rank arrays. Is this a de facto standard, or an accidental implementation detail?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

Additionally, I’d like to report that the same issue also occurs when using nn.RNN instead of nn.LSTM. Specifically, like:

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As we refactor SciPy’s multivariate distributions to align with NumPy’s evolving broadcasting rules, we're uncertain whether `size` should behave uniformly across all distributions. For example, in `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))`, the output shape `(10, 4, 2, 3)` includes the variate dimension `(3,)` as part of the core function signature, while `size` controls only the outer batch dimensions. We want to confirm this is the canonical pattern before applying it to `multivariate_normal` or `dirichlet`, but the documentation doesn't explicitly define this contract for gufunc-like signatures.
original_rephrased_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Modified the script to let the adaptive commit finish; memory was released after an approximate 5‑6 s wait on the local setup.

rephrased_statement: During a debugging session I inadvertently uncovered a non‑trivial numerical inconsistency in PyTorch's `nn.Linear` when operating on half‑precision tensors that are derived via slicing rather than copying.  The reproducible snippet sets a deterministic seed, constructs a `float16` tensor `x1` on the GPU, extracts a delayed view `x2 = x1[:, 2:]`, and verifies their equivalence with `torch.allclose`.  After casting a linear layer to the same dtype, the forward passes `out1 = net(x1)` and `out2 = net(x2)` produce a maximal absolute difference of `tensor(0.0010, ...)` between the sliced portions of `out1` and `out2`.  An `assert torch.allclose` subsequently raises an `AssertionError`.  Repeating the experiment in `bfloat16` magnifies the gap to `0.0078`.  Notably, enforcing contiguity via `x2 = x1[:, 2:].clone()` or switching to `float32` yields a perfect match (`0.`).  Does the PyTorch half‑precision backend intentionally allow this level of drift for strided inputs, or have we uncovered a subtle bug in the conversion or GEMM pipeline?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.

 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s

 CUDA 0.82 s

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Given SciPy's roadmap for extending the multivariate distribution suite, can we guarantee that any new size‑parameter semantics will stay compatible with NumPy's existing and forthcoming multivariate APIs, especially regarding broadcasting of 1‑D or 2‑D parameter arrays?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Given that MPS shows 98% utilization and high power draw during BERT inference, why is performance worse than CPU? I built PyTorch from source with Accelerate.framework, but no ANE activity is visible. Could this be a case where the overhead of memory copies between CPU and GPU domains (even in unified architecture) is dominating computation time for small-to-medium batch sizes?

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: When `executeMPSGraph` runs with `COMMIT_ADAPTIVE` as the `SyncMode`, operations are encoded to the active MPSStream command buffer without immediate commit unless memory pressure triggers a commit.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re adapting SciPy’s multivariate distributions to support broadcasting similar to NumPy’s `multinomial`, but we’re uncertain about the semantics of the `size` parameter. Specifically, does `size=(10, 4, 2)` mean 'generate 10 samples for each of 4×2 parameter combinations', leaving the variate dimension (e.g., 3 for multinomial) to be appended automatically? Or does it intend to fully specify the final output shape? We have no documentation confirming this, and we’re unsure whether this behavior is intentional across distributions or an implementation artifact we should avoid replicating.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Given that torch.backends.mps.is_available() returns True and GPU utilization reaches 98.8 % during the MPS run, I wonder whether the slowdown originates from the choice of BLAS library (Accelerate.framework) or from an unoptimized kernel path in the current nightly PyTorch build; the code reproduces the issue with torch.no_grad() and a batch of 64 inputs, yielding 36 s on MPS compared with 18 s on CPU and 0.82 s on CUDA.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Switching to `SyncMode::COMMIT_AND_WAIT` triggers a commit after each encode, after which the output buffers become eligible for garbage collection and memory usage drops accordingly.
